title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
learning_outcomes: Explain data Cleaning and Preprocessing and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in data Cleaning and Preprocessing to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study data Cleaning and Preprocessing within Data Fundamentals and Preparation. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Data quality and governance shape downstream outcomes. Record where data came from, what it means, and how it was transformed before training.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Preprocessing repairs or standardizes data in ways that should be consistent and reproducible. Learn transformation parameters from the training data only when appropriate, and investigate outliers instead of automatically deleting them.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Missing values
items.text: Inspect missing values, duplicates, and unusual observations before deciding how to handle them. Document the rule and test whether cleaning changes subgroup representation or important information.

items.title: Duplicate records
items.text: Inspect missing values, duplicates, and unusual observations before deciding how to handle them. Document the rule and test whether cleaning changes subgroup representation or important information.

items.title: Incorrect and inconsistent values
items.text: Incorrect and inconsistent values is one of the concepts used to reason about data cleaning and preprocessing. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Outlier investigation
items.text: Inspect missing values, duplicates, and unusual observations before deciding how to handle them. Document the rule and test whether cleaning changes subgroup representation or important information.

items.title: Data normalization
items.text: Scaling transforms numeric features to a common range or statistical scale. Fit scaling parameters on training data only and apply the same learned transformation to validation, test, and production inputs.

items.title: Data standardization
items.text: Scaling transforms numeric features to a common range or statistical scale. Fit scaling parameters on training data only and apply the same learned transformation to validation, test, and production inputs.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what data cleaning and preprocessing takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Data quality and governance shape downstream outcomes. Record where data came from, what it means, and how it was transformed before training.

content_blocks.code:
rows = [{"id": 1, "score": 8}, {"id": 2, "score": None}, {"id": 2, "score": 6}]
seen = set()
clean = []
for row in rows:
    if row["id"] in seen or row["score"] is None:
        continue
    seen.add(row["id"])
    clean.append(row)
print("kept rows:", len(clean))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content.task: Try it yourself: create six synthetic records for data cleaning and preprocessing. Identify a quality issue, document a repeatable handling rule, and show how the rule changes the data without leaking test-set information. The linked practice activity is: Explore a Dataset. hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
